L35: # Revoked but Still Executable: Closing the Authorization-to-Effect Gap with Finality-Bound Revocation
L36: ## 【13†Abstract】
L37: Revocation is often treated as a property of a credential, token, session, grant, policy, or identity record. In consequence-bearing systems, however, an authorization can be completely legitimate when issued and still become unsafe before the authorized operation becomes externally effective. The security question is therefore not only whether revocation exists, but whether a revocation that becomes authoritative before a protected commit is guaranteed to control that commit.
L38: The severity is deployment- dependent, but can be high in financial, administrative, AI-agent, cloud-control, confidential-compute, device, industrial, or other environments where a stale-but-valid authorization can produce an irreversible or externally consequential effect.【14†¶】
L39: This document describes a finality-bound revocation model. A Candidate Act remains in a Non-Effective State after upstream authorization. The authorization is bound to an act-specific revocation basis, such as a protected revocation generation, epoch, status root, or equivalent authority state. Immediately before the protected consequence is committed, a Finality Sink verifies that no applicable revocation, suspension, narrowing, or superseding authorization state has become load-bearing.

L78: Abstract
L79: Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) frameworks enable individuals to receive and present digital credentials in a user-controlled way. Revocation mechanisms ensure that invalid or withdrawn credentials cannot be misused. These revocation mechanisms must be scalable (e.g., at national scale) and preserve core SSI principles such as privacy, user control, and interoperability.
L80: Achieving both is hard, and finding a suitable trade-off remains a key challenge in SSI research.This paper introduces UPPR, a revocation mechanism for One-Show Verifiable Credentials (oVCs) and unlinkable Anonymous Credentials (ACs). Revocations are managed using percredential Verifiable Random Function (VRF) tokens, which are published in a Bloom filter cascade on a blockchain. Holders prove non-revocation via a VRF proof for oVCs or a single Zero-Knowledge Proof for ACs.
L81: The construction prevents revocation status tracking, allows holders to stay offline, and hides issuer revocation behavior. We analyze the privacy properties of UPPR and provide a prototype implementation on Ethereum. Our implementation enables off-chain verification at no cost. On-chain checks cost 0.56–0.84 USD, while issuers pay only 0.00002–0.00005 USD per credential to refresh the revocation state.

L218: On-chain reputation is inherently exposed to Sybil attacks and reciprocal-endorsement farming, in which a small set of agents repeatedly endorse one another to inflate their scores before behaving maliciously toward a third party. Gated registration through accountable real-world operators serves as a first-line barrier to mass identity creation, while collusion detection currently relies on the Oversight Layer.
L219: This reliance on human supervision is a limitation of the present design, with protocol-level countermeasures, such as a registration stake, reputation-weighted endorsements, and discounting reputation from a small recurring set of partners, left to future work.
L220: Newly created agents receive a starting trust score that is either a neutral default or, preferably, derived from the credentials they already hold, so an agent born with a founding VC from its operator and attestations from reputable issuers begins above a bare default. This value reflects no earned history, and discovery filtering combines it with direct inspection of the agent's credentials, weighing both their number and the standing of their issuers.
L221: Because operators and issuers are accountable real-world entities, an agent holding credentials from highly trusted institutions, such as a government body, is more likely to be selected. Numeric reputation then changes through post-interaction endorsements.
L222: ## IMPLEMENTATION
L223: The implementation is built on a hybrid architecture that integrates off-chain components responsible for agentic orchestration with on-chain components responsible for identity verification and authorization. Off-chain agent orchestration is handled by Google's ADK (Google 【30†2025a】), with structured interagent communication carried over the A2A protocol.
L224: The on-chain trust infrastructure is implemented as a Solidity smart contract deployed on the Ethereum Sepolia test network using the Hardhat development framework. Blockchain queries from agent logic are performed via read-only JSON-RPC calls using the Web3.py library, ensuring that registry and reputation queries introduce no chain-state modifications and low latency relative to the A2A communication round-trip.
L225: Agent DIDs are provisioned by authorized operators at deployment time following the W3C DID specification; post-interaction endorsements are structured as W3C VCs signed using the agents' cryptographic key pairs.
L226: ### Agent registry and cryptographic identity
L227: The core on-chain component is the agent registry smart contract, which implements the discovery and reputation infrastructure described in the architecture. Each agent is identified by a unique cryptographic key, with its public component stored on-chain alongside the agent's DID reference, capability metadata, and current reputation score.
L228: Separate smart contracts govern the reputation and incentive logic, automatically processing incoming VC endorsement hashes to update trust scores and trigger reward or penalization rules. The on-chain state is immutable and globally verifiable, ensuring that the capability and reputation information available to any querying agent is consistent and tamper-evident.
L229: ### Blockchain tool for agent-blockchain interaction
L230: A key design decision for the implementation is to encapsulate all blockchain interactions within a dedicated ADK-style tool that any agent in the system can invoke.
L231: Rather than embedding blockchain-specific logic directly into agent code, the tool exposes a clean interface with two categories of operations: read-only queries (e.g., resolving an agent's DID, retrieving capability metadata, reading the current trust score) and state-changing transactions (e.g., submitting a VC endorsement hash, triggering an incentive or penalization update).
L232: Agents call this tool as part of their normal reasoning loop, in the same way they invoke any other capability, without needing to be aware of the underlying blockchain mechanics.
L233: Read-only operations are executed as lightweight JSON-RPC calls that neither modify the chain state nor introduce latency. State-changing operations sign and submit a transaction using the invoking agent's private key, which also constitutes its on-chain identity anchor.
